item.text:
**Assessment**
Mixed, but leaning negative. I found one clear patronage/nepotism case and several signs of coercive or selectively opaque state behavior, while the strongest counterevidence is mostly rhetorical or technocratic rather than proof of durable separation between private interests and state power.

**Accepted Claims**

| Title | Publisher | Date | URL | Claim-level summary | Question IDs |
|---|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Tinubu under fire for appointing son-in-law head of housing agency | BusinessDay | 2024-02-21 | https://businessday.ng/news/article/tinubu-under-fire-for-appointing-son-in-law-head-of-housing-agency/ | Tinubu appointed his son-in-law to lead the Federal Housing Authority. Critics called it nepotism and a breach of the federal-character norm. This is the clearest 2024 counterexample to clean separation of family interest from state appointments. | 7B.3 |
| Nigeria’s President Tinubu picks son-in-law Oyetunde Oladimeji Ojo to run housing agency | BBC News via ecoi.net | 2024-02-16 | https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2104503.html | BBC’s report confirms the appointment of Tinubu’s son-in-law to head the FHA and notes the controversy over favoritism. This reinforces the nepotism concern with independent media corroboration. | 7B.3 |
| Tinubu violated oath of office by appointing son-in-law, says HURIWA | The Guardian Nigeria | 2024-02-19 | https://guardian.ng/news/tinubu-violated-oath-of-office-by-appointing-son-in-law-says-huriwa/ | A rights group alleged the son-in-law appointment reflected deep-rooted nepotism and concentration of strategic appointments among kin. This is advocacy-level criticism, but it directly supports the patronage reading. | 7B.3 |
| President Tinubu Directs Reorganisation of the Bureau of Public Procurement | State House, Abuja | 2024-06-15 | https://statehouse.gov.ng/president-tinubu-directs-reorganisation-of-the-bureau-of-public-procurement/ | Tinubu ordered the BPP chief to resign as part of a reorganization meant to improve efficiency and transparency. This is positive evidence that he sometimes used formal administrative levers to tighten procurement discipline. | 7B.3 |
| President Tinubu: I have no Cabal or Sponsors to Compensate | State House, Abuja | 2024-07-26 | https://statehouse.gov.ng/president-tinubu-i-have-no-cabal-or-sponsors-to-compensate/ | Tinubu explicitly denied owing a cabal or sponsors and said his campaign was self-sponsored. This is relevant counterevidence against a pure loyalty-repayment model, but it is self-assertion rather than independent proof. | 7B.3 |
| ECOWAS’ Hand of Friendship Still Open to Niger, Mali, and Burkina Faso, Says President Tinubu | State House, Abuja | 2024-08-09 | https://statehouse.gov.ng/ecowas-hand-of-friendship-still-open-to-niger-mali-and-burkina-faso-says-president-tinubu/ | Tinubu publicly pushed reconciliation and reintegration in ECOWAS, framing regional security and constitutional government as collective goods. This is positive evidence that foreign policy was being presented in institutional, not personal, terms. | 7B.3 |
| President Tinubu Urges ECOWAS Countries To Ratify, Fully Implement Anti-corruption Protocol | State House, Abuja | 2024-08-19 | https://statehouse.gov.ng/president-tinubu-urges-ecowas-countries-to-ratify-fully-implement-anti-corruption-protocol/ | Tinubu publicly urged implementation of the ECOWAS anti-corruption protocol and expansion of transparent governance structures. This is positive institutional rhetoric, though it does not by itself prove clean separation from domestic patronage. | 7B.3 |
| Nigeria's Tinubu names seven ministers, sacks five in cabinet reshuffle | Reuters via Yahoo News | 2024-10-23 | https://www.yahoo.com/news/nigerias-tinubu-names-seven-ministers-152818783.html | Tinubu reshuffled the cabinet, sacking five ministers, appointing seven new ones, and keeping the finance, defence, and planning portfolios in place. This is weak positive evidence against arbitrary loyalty testing, since the core economic ministries were retained and the move looks like routine executive management. | 7B.3 |
| Nigerian journalist detained over a week under cybercrime law, employer says | Reuters via Yahoo News | 2024-05-09 | https://www.yahoo.com/news/nigerian-journalist-detained-over-week-121429975.html | Police detained investigative journalist Daniel Ojukwu under the cybercrime law after a corruption story. This is negative evidence that truth-tellers could be punished when they exposed elite or state wrongdoing. | 7B.3, 7B.2 |
| Nigeria police charge 4 journalists with cybercrimes for corruption reporting | Committee to Protect Journalists | 2024-10-03 | https://cpj.org/2024/10/nigeria-police-charge-4-journalists-with-cybercrimes-for-corruption-reporting/ | CPJ reported that four journalists were charged under the Cybercrimes Act despite February reforms. This shows the government still tolerated legal pressure on scrutiny late in 2024. | 7B.3, 7B.2 |
| Nigeria | Freedom House | 2024 | https://freedomhouse.org/country/nigeria/freedom-net/2024 | Freedom House reported no internet shutdowns, which is weak positive evidence for openness. But it also documented cyberstalking-law abuse, monitoring of “false information,” and blocking powers, which cut the other way on protecting scrutiny and independent reporting. | 7B.3, 7B.2 |
| FG spent N63.6bn on military equipment in seven months - report | Punch | 2024-08-17 | https://punchng.com/fg-spent-n63-6bn-on-military-equipment-in-seven-months-report/ | The report cited large military-equipment and ammunition spending with weak disclosure. That does not prove personal gain, but it is negative evidence for clean procurement and transparent separation between public security spending and opaque channels. | 7B.3 |

**Search Gap**
- I did not find strong direct public evidence in 2024 that Tinubu used licensing or regulation to advance a personal business interest.
- I also did not find a clear foreign-policy case where a private family or business interest visibly drove a specific Tinubu decision.
- The strongest evidence is concentrated in one nepotism appointment, plus procurement opacity and press repression around corruption reporting.
